findings.location: Terminology Notes section, all three sentences
findings.evidence: You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review.
findings.violation: The section titled Terminology Notes never defines a term. Instead it introduces stipend item, used three times here and nowhere else in the document, while every other section calls the reimbursed object equipment (equipment stipend, equipment cost, equipment category) or refers to the stipend request. A reader cannot tell whether stipend item names the same thing as equipment, the same thing as the request, or a third concept, and the one section meant to resolve that kind of confusion compounds it instead.
findings.fix: Replace stipend item with the term already used elsewhere (equipment, or the stipend request, whichever this section actually means), or add one sentence in this section stating the equivalence explicitly.

findings.location: Program Coordination section, final sentence, and Review Responsibility section, first sentence
findings.evidence: Once approved, the team schedules the reimbursement for the next pay cycle. [Program Coordination] / The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out. [Review Responsibility]
findings.violation: Program Coordination ends by stating that once a request is approved, the benefits team schedules the reimbursement, describing payout as already in motion. The very next section, Review Responsibility, states that the finance office reviews every request over 200 dollars before it pays out, a gating step that would logically happen before or during scheduling, not after it, but the document presents it after scheduling with no signal connecting the two. A reader cannot tell whether the 200-dollar review happens before the team schedules the reimbursement or is a separate, later check the two sections leave unordered.
findings.fix: State the 200-dollar review step, and how it relates to the team's scheduling step, within Program Coordination itself, or move Review Responsibility ahead of Program Coordination's scheduling sentence and add one clause connecting the two steps explicitly.

findings.location: Program Overview, Special Cases, and Questions and Updates sections
findings.evidence: the IT asset group tracks the equipment catalog on the first business day of the month [Program Overview]; The finance liaison publishes the equipment catalog at the start of the fiscal year. [Special Cases]; The benefits team reviews the equipment catalog at the start of the fiscal year. [Questions and Updates]
findings.violation: The same equipment catalog is handled by three differently named actors across the document: the IT asset group tracks it, the finance liaison publishes it, and the benefits team reviews it, with no signal whether these are the same team under three names, three teams sharing one responsibility, or three separate steps in a handoff. A reader who needs to know who actually owns the catalog cannot resolve it from the text.
findings.fix: Name one consistent actor for the equipment catalog throughout, or, if the three roles are genuinely distinct, state the handoff between them explicitly the first time a second actor is introduced.

findings.location: Restrictions and Exceptions section, and Terminology Notes section
findings.evidence: You must keep your equipment in good working condition and we may ask for a brief photo check once a year.
findings.violation: Every other section of the document writes about the reader in the third person (employees, the employee, the manager, the finance office), but Restrictions and Exceptions and Terminology Notes abruptly switch to addressing the reader directly as you and referring to the issuing organization as we, with nothing signaling the change. A reader who has been reading a third-person policy description for six sections may not immediately recognize that you now means them, or may wonder whether these two sections were written for a different audience.
findings.fix: Pick one address mode, direct second person or third-person institutional description, and use it throughout the document, or add one sentence noting that these two sections speak directly to the employee if the switch is intentional.

findings.location: Program Overview section, the document's opening section
findings.evidence: The IT asset group updates the reimbursement log at the start of the fiscal year. A copy of each update goes to the shared benefits folder the same day. Similarly, the IT asset group tracks the equipment catalog on the first business day of the month.
findings.violation: The document's opening section, the first thing a reader sees, describes internal IT and finance recordkeeping cadence that no applying employee needs in order to act. Eligibility, the section that answers the reader's actual first question of whether they qualify, is delayed to second position behind it. The ordering tracks the internal record-update workflow rather than the reader's own task sequence.
findings.fix: Open with Eligibility, or a one-line statement of what the stipend is and who it is for, and move the reimbursement-log and equipment-catalog update cadence into a later, clearly internal-process section such as Program Coordination.

findings.evidence: Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt.
findings.violation: This section restates how to start a request, but it appears as the ninth section, after How to Apply already covered the application process third, and after Reimbursement Amounts and Required Documentation, sections that only make sense once a request already exists. A reader following the document's own task sequence has already applied by the time they reach a section titled Request Steps.
findings.fix: Move Request Steps next to How to Apply, or fold its content into How to Apply directly and remove it as a separate section.
